messages.author: dfd6902445a04230
messages.subject: autodiff for empirical likelihood
parts:
Hi,

I'm looking to implement Bayesian inference for empirical likelihood functions.  To make a long story short, the log-likelihood (upon suppressing the data) is of the form loglik(theta) = f( x = theta, y = lambda(theta) ), where theta are the parameters of interest and for given theta, lambda(theta) is the solution to d/dy f(theta, lambda) = 0.  I don't forsee any difficulties in writing a STAN function, say lambda_calc, which returns the value of lambda(theta).  However, by construction, d/d.theta loglik(theta) is just d/dx f( theta, lambda(theta) ).  I'm wondering whether STAN's autodiff will "know" this or whether I can inform it of this.  I would hate for it to differentiate through the inner workings of lambda_calc...

Thanks,

martin

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: autodiff for empirical likelihood
parts:
I have been thinking about things like this for a long time, but it is not implemented yet. Even if you write a while loop to find the solution to d/dy f(theta, lambda) = 0, Stan won't know the implicit differentiation. Essentially, we need to add the ability to numerically solve general non-linear equations within a Stan program in much the same way we just added the ability to solve ODEs.

Ben

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: autodiff for empirical likelihood
parts:
I don't think there is any way to do it with just Stan code, but it is pretty straightforward (in a particular case) if you write the C++ code.

There is this for implementing new functions in general:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Contributing-New-Functions-to-Stan

In this particular case, you need a function that
  1. Solves for the root of the implicit function with regular double variables. There are many tools in Boost for this.
  2. Returns the solution in special Stan var variables that takes into account the implicit differentiation, i.e. the sensitivities of the solution to the parameters declared in the parameters block. There are many examples of doing this in the Stan library (e.g. softmax.hpp). Technically, you should get it to work with both forward mode and reverse mode autodiff and there are subdirectories under $STAN_HOME/src/stan/agrad for each.

Ben

On Monday, June 29, 2015 at 11:56:25 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
If someone could write the solver and the gradients, it should
be very easy to put in the language.  I don't even understand
what we'd need to do it --- if it's just an ode integrator, then
it'd be great if we could isolate the integrator from the function
because Daniel's currently plugging and playing some alternatives.

There's at least 3 similarish things we could potentially do with a user-defined function in Stan:
  1. integrate it, which we can sort of do already with the ODE stuff but we don't have other quadrature algos
  2. optimize it, which we can't do now but it basically just entails passing a user-defined function to our LBFGS algorithm instead of the log_prob()
  3. solve it (within an interval) for the parameters that cause it to be zero, which we can't do now but there is stuff in Boost and Eigen for that
Ideally, these would all have similar semantics to ODEs in Stan with the functors and all that.

This particular thread is referring to 2). The "likelihood" function involves weights and you have to find the optimal weights given the parameters to evaluate the log-likelihood. There is a review paper about ideas like this here

http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com.ezproxy.cul.columbia.edu/doi/10.1002/9781118771051.ch11/pdf

As for 1), some PDFs involve intractable integrals. For example, equation 4 in

http://academic2.american.edu/~jpnolan/stable/density.ps

I had some C++ code that yields a good numerical approximation of that particular integral but we need a more general framework.

For 3), we can solve some linear systems of equations but have nothing for the nonlinear ones. A simple example where this is needed is (most) inverse CDFs, given 0 < p < 1 and theta, you have to numerically choose x such that F(x|theta) - p = 0. And once you get that x*(p, theta), you have utilize implicit differentiation to ultimately get the derivatives of the log-posterior wrt p and / or theta.

There's more applications, but it is really more of a deal where we need to build on the syntactic framework we used for ODEs.

Ben

None of these features are trivial, even once an interface
has been designed.  The problem is trying to figure out
how they couple with the sampler performance.

(1) This is going to be a nightmare given how hard integration is 
(that’s why we do MCMC in the first place, after all…).  I’m 
hesitant to offer any quadrature that isn’t super robust.

(2) This one is somewhat more straightforward but I think more
subtle than people realize.  Aside from identifiability problems,
there are various regularity conditions required for the derivative
and the optimization criterion to commute, which we need to
compute the derivative of the optimum (as is done the in MML
derivation).  I’m not sure how we can guarantee these conditions
or warn the user if they’re not satisfied.  

Somewhat straightforward to implement but would require a
pretty serious amount of work to make robust methodologically.
A good masters/PhD project.

(3) This is probably the most straightforward theoretically given
the guarantees of the Implicit Function Theorem.  We already
have gradients so we can put together a slick root finder
pretty easily (again, there are always identifiability issues at hand)
and the derivatives of the solution will then be relatively straightforward.

Another relatively self-contained project ideal for students.

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] autodiff for empirical likelihood
parts:
On Tuesday, June 30, 2015 at 4:19:12 AM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
(2) This one is somewhat more straightforward but I think more
subtle than people realize.  Aside from identifiability problems,
there are various regularity conditions required for the derivative
and the optimization criterion to commute, which we need to
compute the derivative of the optimum (as is done the in MML
derivation).  I’m not sure how we can guarantee these conditions
or warn the user if they’re not satisfied.

There are things like MML where the user would write down a conventional log-posterior and then do some complicated optimization thing instead of MCMC. But the OP is referring to something else, where the user is going to do MCMC with informative priors but evaluating the "log-likelihood" entails constrained optimization of a user-defined function. The "likelihood" for observation i is $\frac{w_{i}^{\ast}\left(\theta\right)}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}w_{j}^{\ast}\left(\theta\right)}$.  So the .stan program would be like

functions{
  vector foo(...)
}
data {
  int<lower=1> N;
  int<lower=1> K;
  ...
}
parameters {
  vector[K] theta;
}
model {
  vector[N] log_weights;
  log_weights <- make_log_weights(foo, theta, ...); // entails optimization
  increment_log_prob(log_weights);
  increment_log_prob(-N * log_sum_exp(log_weights));
  theta ~ normal(0,1);
}

So, I am not seeing where MML-like regulatory conditions are needed here. It is like MCMC involving ODEs but with optimization instead of integration of foo.

Ben

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] autodiff for empirical likelihood
parts:
No, I know.  

Let’s say we have parameters theta and there is some 
component of the likelihood of the form

\hat{f} (theta) = max_{phi} g(theta, phi)

We can run an optimizer to get a point value of \hat{f} (theta),
but then what is the derivative, d \hat{f} / d theta that we need
to run our algorithms?

The regularity conditions to which I was referring are those
that ensure that we can do

d/dtheta \hat{f} (theta) 
= d/dtheta max_{phi} g(theta, phi)
= max_{phi} d / dtheta g(theta, phi)

which gives another optimization that we can run.  This is
one way to derive the MML updates, but here has a more
general use.

Not much. The options seem to be
  1. Restrict the models to cases where lambda is an explicit function of theta
  2. Write particular models in C++ where you use Boost to numerically solve for lambda and deal with the derivatives yourself
  3. Implement numerical optimization within .stan programs like for integrate_ode and utilize implicit differentiation

Ben

messages.subject: Re: autodiff for empirical likelihood
parts:
On Friday, July 31, 2015 at 10:33:10 PM UTC-4, MT wrote:

However, As Ben pointed out, the lagrange multiplier is really a function of the original model parameters declared in the stan parameters {} Block.


Yes, that is the key point.
 

To find the lagrange multiplier, It seems like there are 2 useful pursuits:

1) In C++ - Find the lagrange multiplier using built optimizers, say from boost.


This is the better route, and one could even use Stan's LBFGS optimization and / or autodiff. I suspect if integrate_ode() were used as a template, adding an optimize() function would take 1 day to implement, test, and document. There would need to be an implicit differentiation too. But I don't know how to get the parser to generate the C++ code like it does for ODEs.
 

2) Remain in STAN: Doing some further reading, we can actually solve for lambda a brute force way involving control loops and a singular value decomposition. From my understanding, although a default 'optimizer' isn't accessible within stan, control loops and svd are.


Only singular values but in any event, this is much less promising than 1)
 

For both these approaches, it seems crucial to tell stan NOT to rely on autodiff, so the user computed log empirical likelihood and it's gradient can update the log posterior and it's gradient correctly. (Which basically gets at the original post of this thread)


The likelihood would mostly be a log_sum_exp(), which is already pretty-well optimized. But being able to write

w ~ empirical_likelihood();

in Stan programs wouldn't hurt.

Ben

I suspect if integrate_ode() were used as a template, adding an optimize() function would take 1 day to implement, test, and document. There would need to be an implicit differentiation too. But I don't know how to get the parser to generate the C++ code like it does for ODEs.

You're on.  If you write the C++ code, it'll probably be no problem to
deal with the parser side.  What would the syntax look like?

This is actually a .stan program for the Bayesian Exponential Tilted Likelihood of

http://www.jstor.org.ezproxy.cul.columbia.edu/stable/20441164?seq=1#page_scan_tab_contents

which is similar but preferable to the Exponential Likelihood approach mentioned by the OP:

// Literal version of Schennach (2005)
// https://scholar.google.com/citations?view_op=view_citation&hl=en&citation_for_view=tArAJ7sAAAAJ:2osOgNQ5qMEC

functions {
  vector g(vector theta, vector[] X) {
    // implementation varies depending on the moment constraints
  }
  real eq_10(vector eta, vector theta, vector[] X) {
    vector[size(X)] temp;
    for (n in 1:size(X))
      temp[n] <- dot_product(eta, g(theta, X[n]));
    return log_sum_exp(temp);

}
}
data {
  int<lower=1> N;
  int<lower=1> K;

vector[K] X[N];
  int<lower=K> C;
}
parameters {
  vector[K] theta;
}
transformed parameters {
  vector[C] lambda;
  lambda <- rep_vector(0,C);
  /* this needs to be interpreted as "pass guesses for lambda to the first argument of eq_10" */
  lambda <- minimize(eq_10, theta, X); // calls LBFGS then does an implicit differentiation
}
model {
  vector[N] log_w; // unnormalized version of equation 9
  for (n in 1:N) log_w[n] <- dot_product(lambda, g(theta, X[n]));
  increment_log_prob(log_w);
  increment_log_prob(-N * log_sum_exp(log_w));
  // prior on theta
}

The integrate_ode function has a very particular signature based on the structure of ODE problems (that we can solve), whereas the less structured minimize(function, vector, ...) and maximize(function, vector, ...) functions should probably overload the trailing arguments to provide more flexibility in passing the data. But in this case, only a matrix-like X is needed.

Ben

On Sunday, August 2, 2015 at 12:34:54 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
So is the signature to minimize always this

  vector[] minimize(f, vector, vector[]);

I think minimize should always return a vector rather than a vector[]. Its first argument should always be the function to minimize and its second argument a parameter vector. Beyond that, the data could have any structure but for the model in the Schennach (2005) paper it would be a vector[].

where f has signature
 
  real f(vector, vector, vector[]);
Definitely returning a real and the first two arguments should be vectors. Beyond that, there is the same issue with the (lack of) data structure.

If so, that'll be a piece of cake to drop into the language.
If not, is there a way to do something like we did for ode_integrate()
to give it a universal signature?

Maybe we just have to let the trailing arguments be a real[], int[], vector[], and matrix[] and permit some to be zero-sized. I guess that is better than all combinations thereof.

At some point, we might want to do one-dimensional optimization, in which case it would be

real minimize(f, real, vector, ...)

where f is

real f(real, vector, ...)

Ben
